#5156. Bitcoin miners’ daily revenue per unit of computing power falls 8.7%

Hashprice fell from $35.99 to $32.86 per PH/s/day in the November 2 weekly snapshot; October 30 forwards implied little network growth through December.

Bitcoin miners face weak dollar revenue even as the mining forward market priced in little additional competition through December, according to an October 30 analysis by mining data platform Hashrate Index. That could give miners a respite after difficulty’s 16.4% rebound.

Hashprice, the expected daily mining revenue for a unit of computing power, stood at $32.86 per petahash per second per day on November 2 at 18:00 UTC. That was down 8.7% from $35.99 a week earlier, according to the latest completed weekly snapshot.

Hashrate Index, Luxor’s mining data and research platform, put implied network computing power at 1,056 exahashes per second in November and 1,059 in December in its October 30 analysis. Both were near the approximately 1,062 EH/s average over the mining epoch that ended October 29.

Those are forward-implied levels, rather than observed future hashrate or scheduled difficulty changes. The linked September methodology assumes transaction fees of about 0.02 BTC per block when translating contract prices into implied network growth. Different fee outcomes can therefore change that interpretation.

The curve’s flattening followed a rise in difficulty from 127.45 trillion before September 19’s adjustment to 148.36 trillion on October 29. A pause would leave miners competing at that elevated level.

The November 2 update put average forward hashprice at $33.04 per PH/s/day for November through April 2027. This is an indicative revenue benchmark for that period, with actual execution dependent on agreed contract terms.

The October 30 curve implied nearly flat network growth. November 2’s revenue snapshot shows why a pause alone cannot repair margins.

The revenue rate moves with benchmark inputs, while power costs and actual output determine the margin.

A matched, performing hedge stabilizes the covered benchmark rate; operating costs and production remain exposed.

Stable competition and a forward hedge address different risks; neither fixes operating profit.

In Luxor’s cash-settled contract, a seller receives the difference when the daily index falls below the agreed price and owes the difference when it rises above it. Matching the quantity and dates to actual output matters: the hedge does not ensure the machines keep producing.

A deliverable forward instead provides upfront buyer payment against delivery to Luxor’s mining pool, subject to seller credit checks and possible delivery margin. Luxor is the counterparty to both sides, and its order book displays buying and selling interest that its team must confirm as trades.

For operators with fixed dollar power costs, stabilizing the dollar revenue rate on matched output can improve cash-flow planning. Higher-cost fleets still need that revenue to cover electricity and other expenses; more efficient fleets have more room between gross receipts and costs.

Dollar hashprice also depends on Bitcoin’s price, fees and subsidy, alongside difficulty. Even if competition holds steady, weaker Bitcoin pricing or fees can reduce unhedged revenue.

#5154. Crypto Docs Host GitBook Hit by AI Agent Security Breach, Urges Users to Rotate Keys

Crypto Docs Host GitBook Hit by AI Agent Security Breach, Urges Users to Rotate Keys

GitBook, a documentation platform widely used by cryptocurrency projects, has disclosed a security breach involving AI agents that allowed an attacker to gain access to some of its infrastructure credentials, forcing the company to shut down services and revoke customer access tokens.

In a security disclosure published today, the company described the incident as “a sophisticated, highly targeted attack using AI agents.” The attacker gained unauthorized access at 7 p.m. Central European Time on November 2, according to GitBook, which said it detected the intrusion immediately and moved to contain it.

The reference to AI agents is significant. Unlike traditional chatbots that simply respond to questions, AI agents can carry out sequences of actions, interact with software, and perform tasks with limited human supervision, making them potentially useful to attackers trying to automate parts of a cyberattack. Some are even capable of acting autonomously and even against their guidelines, as OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s experiments have proven.

GitBook has not explained exactly how the attacker used these tools, which AI systems were involved, or how the credentials were obtained. Its disclosure also does not establish that GitBook's own AI products were responsible for the intrusion.

The company took its application and documentation sites requiring authentication offline while securing its infrastructure. It also kept publicly available documentation accessible through cached copies for as long as possible, allowing visitors to continue reading previously saved versions of pages even while the underlying systems were unavailable.

A separate status notice acknowledged that GitBook was experiencing downtime affecting its published documentation sites and editor. By Tuesday afternoon, GitBook said its application, API, and published documentation were accessible again, although some services could remain degraded during recovery.

GitBook is effectively an online instruction manual for software products. Cryptocurrency projects use platforms like it to publish technical explanations, developer instructions, and guides that help users understand everything from connecting software to interacting with decentralized financial applications.

The documents themselves are often public, but the systems that maintain them can connect to private accounts and external services. Those connections depend on credentials that are supposed to remain secret, and GitBook says some of them may have been exposed.

Its investigation identified several potentially affected categories, including integration tokens, Git Sync secrets used to connect documentation with code repositories, and API tokens that allow software to communicate with GitBook automatically.

The incident has already prompted a response from the cryptocurrency industry, where documentation websites often serve as an important source of official instructions.

Decentralized exchange PancakeSwap temporarily disabled its documentation following news of the incident, although it said its own systems had not been compromised.

In a public statement, PancakeSwap said its “docs are not compromised and [the] PancakeSwap app is not affected.” The exchange nevertheless took its documentation offline as a precaution and redirected visitors to its homepage.

PancakeSwap reminded users that its documentation does not require them to perform wallet transactions, warning that “docs never ask you to connect your wallet or approve tokens.”

PancakeSwap subsequently announced that its documentation was back online after being moved from GitBook to infrastructure under its own control, with existing documentation links continuing to work.

GitBook says it blocked the attacker, addressed the vulnerabilities involved, replaced its own infrastructure credentials, and invalidated customer API tokens. But customers using GitBook alongside other services still have work to do.

The company's instructions begin with “rotate any existing GitBook API tokens,” meaning customers should replace their old digital access keys with newly generated ones.

GitBook also instructed customers to replace third-party API tokens and secrets used to connect external tools to its platform, including credentials associated with published integrations. Users of its Model Context Protocol, or MCP, server must authenticate again; MCP is a system that allows AI assistants and other software tools to connect to services such as GitBook.

American Riot Platforms Inc. (RIOT) sold off 79% of its Bitcoin in the third quarter of 2026, redirecting capital toward building infrastructure for artificial intelligence. According to a fresh financial report, the company reduced its cryptocurrency reserves from 11,380 to 2,418 BTC.

In total, over the first nine months of the year, Riot sold 20,264 BTC on the market, receiving about $1.5 billion for them. This money went toward financing a major technological shift: the company's free energy capacity is being repurposed for high-performance computing needs.

Riot shares reacted to the session open with a sharp jump to $16.20, after which they stabilized in the $15.45–$15.50 range, holding positions on elevated volumes.

The main incentive for selling the cryptocurrency was a 15-year agreement to lease ready-made sites and capacities (powered land lease) totaling 910 MW at the Corsicana campus in Texas. The strategic partner was the Frontier AI Lab (Anthropic) laboratory.

The initial cost of the contract is estimated at $28 billion, and the average annual rent at the start will be about $1.8 billion. Taking into account other projects, Riot's total long-term revenue in the data center segment has reached $38 billion, and the total controlled capacity is 1,151 MW.

Riot CEO Jason Les noted that the agreement is structured as a triple-net lease. Under its terms, the client itself purchases and maintains the computing equipment. For Riot, this reduces construction costs by roughly half compared to standard Tier 3 data centers. As a result, the company will be able to do without issuing new shares and diluting investors' stakes.

The shift in focus is occurring against the backdrop of falling margins in classic mining. Riot's quarterly revenue from cryptocurrency mining fell by 28% — to $116 million, although the company actually mined 1,637 BTC.

Nevertheless, total quarterly revenue held at $181.4 million (+1% year-over-year), outpacing market forecasts. Net profit amounted to $4.03 million.

To optimize its balance sheet, the company fully closed its $200 million credit line with Coinbase, returning 5,821 BTC from collateral. Riot ended the quarter with free liquidity of $950.2 million (including cash and the remainder of the cryptocurrency). The balance sheet retains 2,418 BTC, which may also go under the hammer in the fourth quarter to finance the Texas construction.

The voters have spoken. Now, the focus shifts to how investors react.

The chances of Democrats winning have already increased to 99%, and today’s outcome has seen them sweep both houses of Congress (Senate and House of Representatives). The question now is whether this shift brings some certainty to the market and allows Bitcoin to recover, or will it add another layer of volatility.

According to the latest Santiment data, Bitcoin retail sentiment has become increasingly bearish after the election results. The chart below shows that there are now only 0.51 bullish comments for every bearish comment. With many traders viewing the Republicans as more crypto-friendly, the Democratic sweep has added another layer of uncertainty to an already weak market structure.

Notably, this uncertainty is now showing up across both on-chain and technical indicators.

According to CryptoQuant, Bitcoin’s bounce from recent lows appears to be slowing, with low spot demand and prolonged liquidations taking Bitcoin towards $76,800. Put simply, there is some spot buying, but it isn’t strong enough to offset the selling and liquidation from the futures market. Meanwhile, BTC dominance has faced its third rejection near the 61% range, failing to break higher. This signals fading relative strength.

Together, Bitcoin [BTC] slipping below $77k, weak on-chain momentum, and increasingly bearish retail sentiment are creating a very fragile market structure as investors digest the Democratic sweep. Therefore, is the recent rally in the Bitcoin Fear and Greed Index simply a case of the bears taking a break before sentiment falls into “extreme” fear as the Bitcoin crash narrative takes hold?

Bitcoin’s weak demand, falling dominance, and bearish retail sentiment point to continued market pressure despite the recent sentiment recovery.

The Fear and Greed Index has bounced over 30%, but buying strength remains weak, leaving room for another Bitcoin sell-off.

#5150. US stock perpetuals win clearance, but stock-market halts can still block exits

Kalshi’s scheduled closures prevent opening and closing positions; Coinbase’s filed halt rules show how stock-linked perpetuals inherit equity-market restrictions.

The CFTC said on Nov. 3 that US stock perpetual futures could begin trading on eligible regulated exchanges. These contracts track share prices without a fixed expiration date, but holders remain subject to stock-market halt rules that can interrupt an exit.

Chairman Michael Selig said the contracts had been deemed approved under Regulation 40.3. Eligible venues are designated contract markets also notice-registered with the SEC as securities exchanges, bringing the products into the agencies' joint security-futures framework.

Kalshi says it now offers single-stock perpetuals, with no expiration date, but explicitly warns that they do not trade 24/7. Markets follow schedules with regular closures, and customers cannot open or close positions while a market is closed. Access requires a perpetuals application and educational tutorial; leverage depends on the stock and position size.

For Coinbase, the individual CFTC product record still displayed “Approval Pending” when checked Nov. 4, while the SEC's rulemaking index marked its separate customer-margin proposal withdrawn. Those entries do not overturn the Nov. 3 announcement, but neither establishes a Coinbase customer launch or final terms.

Coinbase's September filing describes cash-settled futures on stocks and ETF shares, without ownership of the underlying shares. Its product submission uses AAPL as a representative specification and makes listing contingent on approvals. Its proposed controls apply to Coinbase's design, rather than setting the terms for every venue.

Securities industry trade group SIFMA's Nov. 2 letter sought further review of proposals from Bitnomial, Coinbase, Kalshi and Nadex, raising concerns about manipulation, thin-liquidity trading and classification.

Under the security-futures halt requirement, a future on a single security must stop trading whenever that security is under a regulatory halt, subject to an applicable exemption. The agencies' joint-rule explanation says exemptions from both sets of requirements are needed.

These controls protect investors by allowing information to circulate and markets to regain order. Their immediate consequence is that an affected holder cannot use a closing trade in the halted contract to reduce exposure.

Buying or selling the same stock, or using its options, cannot be assumed to solve that problem: those markets generally honor the underlying regulatory halt too. A broader-market instrument might remain available during a company-specific interruption, but it leaves company-specific risk.

A venue-only derivatives outage presents a different case. If the cash market or another relevant instrument remains open and accessible, a separate trade may offset some exposure. That is a conditional hedge, dependent on access and liquidity, and it leaves the original perpetual open.

Coinbase's filed Rule 1207 would subject its contracts to US equity market-wide circuit breakers and coordinated halts, while also allowing restrictions for corporate actions, market disruptions and index-price or data outages. Reopening would follow the end of the halt condition and an exchange determination that resumption meets investor-protection and orderly-market requirements. The underlying stock reopening would not, by itself, promise an immediate futures exit.

Neither a fallback price nor a funding pause closes the position or guarantees a trade at the reference value. #5149. Justin Sun Accuses Trump-Backed World Liberty of Using UAE Ties to Escape Federal Court

Justin Sun Accuses Trump-Backed World Liberty of Using UAE Ties to Escape Federal Court

Justin Sun’s legal fight with World Liberty Financial now hinges on a question of nationality.

The Tron founder said Tuesday on X that his lawyers have asked a federal court in California to sanction the Trump family-backed crypto venture over how long it took to disclose that its ownership chain gives it citizenship in the United Arab Emirates.

Sun says he is one of World Liberty’s earliest and largest investors. He agreed in November 2024 to buy $30 million of its WLFI tokens and later raised his total investment to $45 million.

In April, he sued the company, alleging it misled him into investing and then unlawfully froze his tokens. World Liberty has fired back in court, alleging that Sun shorted WLFI and drove down its price.

The current dispute turns on a technical point. Sun chose to sue in federal court, which can hear cases between parties from different places but generally can’t hear a foreign plaintiff’s case against a foreign defendant.

As Sun explained it, a company like World Liberty takes on the citizenship of each of its owners, so a single foreign owner makes the whole company foreign for those purposes.

According to Sun, World Liberty’s initial court disclosure listed only itself, with Florida as its sole citizenship. A judge signaled at an August hearing that some of Sun’s claims should stay in open court rather than go to arbitration.

Less than a week later, Sun says, the company amended the disclosure to list 22 members in its ownership chain, with citizenship in Florida, Delaware, Puerto Rico, and the UAE. World Liberty now argues that the federal court lacks jurisdiction over the case, according to Sun.

Sun argues the late disclosure was a tactic to move the case out of federal court, and his motion seeks to make World Liberty and its lawyers bear the cost. He contrasted the company’s position with its own marketing, posting excerpts from World Liberty’s “gold paper” that describe it as “an American, tax-paying, corporation.”

Once the sanctions motion is resolved, Sun said, he will refile his lawsuit in California state court. “I will keep fighting for the transparency this community deserves,” he wrote.

The feud has played out publicly for months. Sun has criticized how World Liberty treats its investors and alleged that the company threatened to burn his WLFI tokens.

#5148. XRP Ledger Activates New Amendment to Strengthen Network

The XRP Ledger (XRPL) network recently activated a new amendment that helps secure the network by resolving potential security weaknesses and making some existing functionalities more robust and reliable.

This latest amendment, called fixCleanup3_4_0, was activated on Nov. 4, bringing a series of technical updates that include fixes for token issuance, automated market makers (AMMs), lending functionalities, and other parts of the XRP Ledger network.

A fix for a potential security weak point related to token issuance on the XRP Ledger network is a critical aspect of the latest amendment.

As explained in the official documentation of the XRP Ledger network, this update addresses a potential weakness related to delegated permissions that could allow some accounts to issue tokens when they are only allowed to destroy them.

On the XRP Ledger, token issuers can grant permissions to other accounts to perform certain tasks. For example, a stablecoin issuer could delegate permission to burn tokens to another account when customers want to redeem them.

With the latest amendment, the XRP Ledger network addresses this security weakness by preventing a zero-balance, burn-only delegated payment from resulting in the issuance of new tokens.

On top of addressing token issuance permissions, there's more to the fixCleanup3_4_0 amendment.

As explained in the official XRP Ledger network documentation, the fixCleanup3_4_0 update brings several fixes to decentralized trading, asset management, and transaction processing.

For automated market makers (AMMs), this latest update prevents some invalid auction bids and makes some improvements to how liquidity withdrawals and token clawbacks work.

It also brings some fixes for potential unexpected calculation errors or rounding issues that could occur in some cases.

These changes are supposed to make things more predictable when it comes to liquidity pools and avoid potential failures that could happen in some cases.

Another significant aspect of these changes concerns Single Asset Vaults and the proposed native lending infrastructure on the XRP Ledger.

As explained, this amendment brings some improvements to how rounding is handled when assets enter or exit vaults.

The idea is to ensure that transactions do not result in more or fewer assets being transferred than they should.

Bitcoin has risen after every US midterm since 2010, although previous elections triggered brutal selloffs before the cryptocurrency recovered.

Bitcoin surged more than 5% from its election-night low to reclaim $80,000 for the first time since Binance's record hack.

The cryptocurrency extended its recovery from approximately $75,600 on Wednesday, shaking off concerns that Democrats' takeover of Congress would undermine President Donald Trump's crypto-friendly agenda.

According to CoinGlass data, this rally liquidated $453.32 million in the past hour, with most of the losses coming from short traders. These losses reach $913.34 million over the past 24 hours.

The rally comes less than a week after Binance suffered a $6.34 billion security breach that sent shockwaves through the digital asset market, triggering withdrawals and intensifying an already difficult period for Bitcoin investors.

James Butterfill, head of research at CoinShares, told CryptoSlate that the Democratic sweep had largely been priced into Bitcoin before the election, creating room for a relief rally as political uncertainty dissipated.

His assessment reflects a growing distinction between the potential consequences of divided government for the wider crypto industry and Bitcoin itself.

Butterfill expects Democratic control to complicate efforts to advance the CLARITY Act, while potential investigations into Trump-linked cryptocurrency businesses could divert political attention from regulatory reform.

However, he argued that exchanges, token issuers and other companies requiring new regulatory permissions would be more vulnerable to those developments than Bitcoin.

He said that the cryptocurrency's direction remains more closely tied to real yields, dollar liquidity and exchange-traded product flows.

The broader financial markets have already begun reflecting that shift in attention.

According to institutional trading platform Talos, Bitcoin's DVOL, a gauge of expected volatility, declined 6%, while Wall Street's VIX fell 10% as reduced uncertainty encouraged systematic buying across risk assets.

The retreat in volatility coincided with a weaker dollar and declining Treasury yields, providing a more favorable backdrop for Bitcoin's recovery.

On-chain data suggests the rally is arriving as the selling pressure that dominated Bitcoin's recent decline begins to weaken.

CryptoQuant analyst Darkfost said the firm's seller exhaustion model has fallen to levels historically associated with bear-market lows.

The indicator compares the proportion of Bitcoin supply held at a profit with average monthly volatility to assess whether existing holders still have enough incentive to keep selling.

Its latest reading follows a correction of more than 10% from Bitcoin's previous high, during which short-term holders appear to have realized profits and reduced their exposure.

Previous episodes of similarly depressed selling activity have coincided with the formation of market bottoms, although the indicator offers no assurance that prices will immediately recover.

Darkfost identified a critical weakness in the current market: buyers have yet to demonstrate the same conviction as the sellers who recently exited. He said:

While the retreat in selling pressure has allowed Bitcoin to recover above $80,000, sustaining that advance will require fresh capital to absorb any renewed profit-taking.

Bitcoin's latest recovery also coincides with a historical pattern that has delivered substantial gains following every US midterm election since 2010.

CryptoQuant data shows the flagship crypto asset has risen over the subsequent 12 months in all four election cycles, generating a median return of 63%.

Those gains occurred under different political arrangements, including the 2018 midterms, when Democrats captured the House while Republicans retained the Senate.

Bitcoin gained 45.8% over the following year, while the comparable returns after the 2014 and 2022 elections reached 36.8% and 80.8%, respectively.

However, those annual figures conceal significant losses suffered by investors who bought immediately after the votes.

The 2014, 2018 and 2022 votes followed major bear markets, meaning the subsequent rallies unfolded as Bitcoin emerged from steep declines.

That relationship faces a different test in 2026.

Bitcoin entered Tuesday's election with a 20.4% gain over the preceding three months, compared with losses of 44% in 2014, 8.3% in 2018 and 16.5% in 2022.

That leaves this year's market in a materially different position from the previous three cycles, potentially weakening the relevance of the historical post-election returns.

Talos' seasonal figures provide another complication. Bitcoin lost 7.4% in October, and November subsequently recorded declines in three of the five previous years when October ended lower, including 2018 and 2025.

That is why Kelly Ye, Talos' head of research, cautioned against extrapolating the initial relief rally into a sustained recovery. She said:

#5145. Ripple Executive Reveals Massive Growth of Company's London Hub

According to Ripple's UK and Europe Managing Director, Cassie Craddock, Ripple’s London office has expanded significantly over the last decade to become Ripple’s largest international hub outside the U.S.

“When we moved into our current office in 2018, there were 2 floors, and a lot of empty desks. Now we’re on 3 floors and full on all the desks. We’re now over capacity,” she wrote on X.

Craddock's comments came after she took part in a fireside chat at the British Residence in New York as part of Ripple’s Swell conference.

She revealed that Ripple chose to focus on London early on, given the UK's strong capital markets, mature legal system, experienced regulators and concentration of financial talent.

However, she added that regulatory uncertainty had previously limited the company’s capacity to build more relationships with leading U.K. financial institutions.

Ripple's story in the U.K. capital began on March 21, 2016, when the San Francisco-based company officially announced the launch of its first office in London, located in Canary Wharf.

Back then, the expansion was meant to accommodate the growing interest of European banks in distributed ledger technology and cross-border settlement solutions.

Ripple incorporated its U.K. entity in April 2016 under the name Ripple Europe Ltd. (later changed to Ripple Markets UK Ltd. in August 2022).

Ripple continued to expand its ties to U.K. financial institutions in the following years.

In April 2018, Santander introduced its new international payments app, One Pay FX, which used Ripple’s xCurrent technology.

In February 2022, Ripple announced a partnership with London-based payments company Modulr to make it easier to send cross-border payments to the UK and Europe.

Moreover, Ripple has played a role in developing the research landscape for blockchain in the U.K. In January 2026, Ripple shared that it had pledged more than £5M to UK universities under its University Blockchain Research Initiative.

One of the major milestones for Ripple in the U.K. occurred on Jan. 9, when Ripple received an Electronic Money Institution license and cryptoasset registration from the Financial Conduct Authority. The authorizations enabled Ripple to extend its regulated cross-border payment services to UK institutions.

In February, Ripple also secured a partnership with Aviva Investors to explore the tokenization of traditional investment funds.

This work resulted in the launch of a tokenized share class of Aviva Investors’ £22bn Sterling Liquidity Fund on the XRP Ledger on Oct. 26.

The surge in Cash Cat’s price has perpetual traders at its center. CoinGlass showed that the Funding Rate surged significantly, reaching a high of 0.0432% as of November 4, indicating that traders are opening more long positions than shorts.

#5141. Kamino links most of CEO’s KMNO vesting to valuation while holders have no foundation revenue claim

The CEO’s vesting incentive and a $20 million growth commitment leave capital allocation between foundation earnings and any future holder benefit.

Michael Weisz, CEO of Kamino, has tied most of his KMNO allocation to sustained token valuations, according to the Solana lending protocol’s November 3 disclosure. The same announcement tells holders that owning the token gives them no claim on foundation revenue, distributions or equity.

Kamino’s November 3 release describes both the CEO’s incentive arrangement and a $20 million foundation commitment to support its long-term growth plans over the next 24 months. It leaves capital allocation as the step between money accruing to the foundation and any future financial benefit for holders.

Most of Weisz’s KMNO allocation vests only when progressively higher valuation milestones are reached and sustained, the release says. A temporary increase in price does not satisfy the requirement.

That condition concerns most of his allocation. The release does not say that every founder, contributor or investor allocation follows the same rules, and it supplies neither the numerical milestones nor the period for which each must be sustained.

For holders, the incentive aligns part of the CEO’s compensation with sustained token valuations.

Kamino says the foundation has no shareholders, members or beneficiaries, operates under an independent board, and receives all onchain and offchain revenue and intellectual property. Its description places the protocol’s earnings and the foundation’s broader resources within one organization.

The release then states the limit on what that structure means for holders: “KMNO is not a claim on Foundation revenue, distributions or equity.”

DefiLlama’s Kamino data, captured at 20:10 UTC on November 3, makes the economic distinction concrete. Over the preceding 30 days, it recorded $5 million in fees, $607,996 in protocol revenue and $0 in tracked holder revenue.

Each number answers a different question. Fees measure charges generated by tracked activity. Protocol revenue measures the portion retained by the protocol. Holder revenue tracks value reaching holders, rather than assuming everything the protocol earns reaches tokenholders.

For Kamino’s lending products, DefiLlama includes interest, liquidation charges and origination charges in fees. Revenue includes interest spreads, part of liquidation charges and all origination charges; for liquidity products, it includes the protocol’s share of liquidity fees.

Reported trailing-30-day figures. Bar lengths compare $607,996 revenue with $4.67m fees (revenue/fees = 0.130192; desktop 620 and 80.72 units, mobile 310 and 40.36). Organization connectors describe issuer-reported relationships, not a quantified money transfer.

Protocol data is not a foundation financial statement. Zero tracked holder revenue does not measure every holder benefit. Foundation governance, revenue accrual and plans are issuer disclosures; no price outcome or future distribution is assumed.

The $5 million fee total therefore cannot be read as foundation income available for distribution. Even the narrower $607,996 protocol-revenue figure is not a complete statement of foundation earnings, particularly given Kamino’s description of offchain revenue accruing there too.

KMNO’s market snapshot gives scale to the holder-value question: at 20:12 UTC on November 3, CryptoSlate displayed a price of about $0.034, a $200 million market capitalization and $20 million in 24-hour trading volume.

Kamino says the foundation holds reserves beyond its $20 million growth commitment. That commitment describes spending on expansion over two years, rather than a distribution to tokenholders or revenue already earned.

For someone evaluating KMNO, protocol revenue shows what tracked operations retain. Assessing a future holder benefit requires a further explanation of how foundation resources would be allocated, including what is spent on growth, retained in reserves or used in a potential token-support program.

The release cautions that future plans, including potential programs supporting KMNO, may change. Holders can assess the growth commitment and executive alignment now, but any future program will need its own terms before they can judge what benefit it delivers.

#5140. CrowdStrike Launches AI Agent 'Kill Switch,' Plans to Acquire Fiddler AI

CrowdStrike Launches AI Agent 'Kill Switch,' Plans to Acquire Fiddler AI

CrowdStrike has introduced an AI agent kill switch designed to stop unauthorized activity inside corporate networks, alongside plans to acquire AI observability startup Fiddler as businesses give increasingly autonomous software access to their systems.

The cybersecurity company announced the launch Tuesday at its Fal.Con Europe 2026 conference in Barcelona, expanding its Falcon Guardian security platform with controls that let administrators intervene when AI agents stray beyond their assigned tasks.

The move tackles a problem companies face as they deploy AI systems capable of executing code, accessing sensitive information, and interacting with business applications. Unlike conventional chatbots, these agents can perform sequences of actions with limited human oversight, potentially causing damage even when nobody has deliberately attacked them.

In practice, an agent authorized to organize corporate files might misinterpret its instructions, follow malicious directions embedded in a document, or execute a command its operator never intended. The same access that makes autonomous agents useful can also make their mistakes expensive.

The new AI Kill Switch gives security administrators a way to interrupt an agent's activity without waiting for it to complete its task. According to CrowdStrike's technical explanation, the currently available mechanism works through AI gateways, which can block an agent's access to the models powering its decisions.

The initial release does not yet provide every type of containment CrowdStrike has described. The company plans to expand the feature to terminate agent processes directly on endpoints and coordinate restrictions across cloud environments and other enterprise systems.

An authorized administrator triggers the kill switch, and the action is recorded in an audit trail. CrowdStrike also describes controls to prevent terminated agents from restarting and restrict their network access, with broader enforcement capabilities still under development.

The company is adding protections at other points where agents operate. Falcon Guardian can inspect agent prompts and apply policies to tools including Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, GitHub Copilot, Microsoft 365 Copilot, Cursor, and OpenCode.

The risk is already well documented. As Decrypt previously reported, Microsoft researchers identified a vulnerability in Anthropic's Claude Code GitHub Action that could have allowed attackers to manipulate the coding agent into exposing sensitive credentials through malicious repository content. Anthropic subsequently patched the flaw but Crowdstrike’s solution would be more extensive.

CrowdStrike also signed an agreement to acquire Fiddler AI, a company specializing in monitoring AI models and explaining their behavior.

The deal values Fiddler at roughly $400 million, according to The Wall Street Journal. CrowdStrike has not publicly disclosed the acquisition price, although it said the transaction would be paid primarily in cash, with some stock subject to vesting conditions.

Fiddler's technology addresses a related problem that a kill switch alone cannot solve: understanding what an AI agent was doing before something went wrong, and whether its actions were appropriate in the first place.

Its software evaluates agents before deployment, traces their decisions and tool calls, and monitors changes in behavior after they begin operating. These records can help security teams investigate unexpected actions or provide evidence to auditors.

CrowdStrike expects to complete the Fiddler acquisition during the fourth quarter of fiscal 2027, which ends January 31, 2027, subject to customary closing conditions. Its expanded endpoint kill-switch capabilities have not yet received a specific release date.

#5139. Aave and Lido lose $1.7B in massive DeFi capital drop after the Binance hack

Binance's $6.34 billion hack strained DeFi lending as stablecoin supply shrank by over $10 billion and major protocols lost billions in TVL.

Binance's security breach hit a crypto market whose stablecoin market was already shrinking, as DeFiLlama's dashboard put stablecoin market capitalization at $293.8 billion by Nov. 3, down over $10 billion in 30 days.

Binance's Nov. 3 report estimated that approximately $6.34 billion in assets were impacted on October 29 and said the company would absorb the financial impact.

The exchange's Oct. 29 incident added a separate shock to decentralized lending when an exploiter-linked wallet supplied USDT to the Aave lending protocol.

Aave's risk service provider LlamaRisk reported that an exploiter-linked wallet supplied 60 million USDT and borrowed 19,762 units of Wrapped Ethereum (WETH), worth about $44.6 million at the time.

Its Oct. 30 assessment described the position as overcollateralized and subject to normal liquidation, and said it did not put suppliers at risk.

Guardians subsequently froze 175 Aave V3 reserves and 117 V4 reserves. New supply and borrowing stopped in frozen reserves, while repayments, withdrawals and liquidations remained enabled.

Suppliers could withdraw available tokens, but fresh deposits could not replace them. LlamaRisk said withdrawals pushed some large reserves to 92%-100% utilization, meaning almost all supplied funds were borrowed. Borrowing costs rose, and stewards temporarily reduced the upper part of the interest-rate curves.

The affected reserves had reopened by Oct. 31, and LlamaRisk reported on its Nov. 2 update the restoration of specified non-stablecoin collateral settings and said affected reserves had returned to pre-incident rate curves on Nov. 1.

USDT, USDC, and USDT0 still had zero collateral borrowing power in affected configurations.

Among the large protocols examined, Aave recorded the biggest dollar decline between Oct. 27 and Nov. 3. Its dated daily total value locked (TVL) fell by about $1 billion, and Lido followed with a $713 million decline.

Falling token prices can reduce TVL without depositors moving assets, so a smaller TVL does not by itself establish either capital flight or insolvency.

USDT and USDC accounted for about $8.4 billion of the implied 30-day market-cap decline, based on DeFiLlama's rounded values and percentage changes.

DeFiLlama's separate historical series, which has different coverage from the dashboard, fell from $308.8 billion on Oct. 4 to $303.3 billion on Oct. 27.

Issuer redemptions exchange circulating stablecoins for fiat, differing from moving tokens off an exchange or between wallets. Freezing stolen tokens also does not automatically remove them from supply.

The practical risk is the amount of liquidity available where they need it. Thinner trading pools can produce more slippage for the same trade, lending withdrawals can raise borrowing costs, and falling collateral prices increase liquidation exposure.

Conditions would look healthier with renewed stablecoin net issuance, lending deposits returning, lower reserve utilization with more withdrawable tokens, and steadier collateral prices. A rebound in dollar TVL alone would not show that lending cash had returned.

#5138. Librería de Satoshi Rebrands to ISMOS, Launches Global Platform to Train One Million Bitcoin Developers

Librería de Satoshi, the technical education organization, recently announced the launch of its global platform as they rebrand to ISMOS and shows off a new website. The organization aims to expand its Bitcoin and open-source developer education program throughout the world, creating local hubs across the world and delivering education programs in local languages.Since 2021, ISMOS has reached more than 3,665 people in more than 40 countries and has financially supported 30 open-source developers, according to a press release shared with Bitcoin Magazine.

“Talent is universal; opportunity is not. I founded Librería de Satoshi because I experienced the language barrier in Bitcoin firsthand. ISMOS takes that mission worldwide, so that the next great developer can come from anywhere,” said Dulce Villarreal, CEO and founder of ISMOS.

What began as a Bitcoin school for Spanish speakers is today a technical education ecosystem and a complete training path for freedom technologies and open-source developers. ISMOS brings together educators and technology creators: a space to learn and teach with “Freedom Tech values, in more languages, more regions, and more disciplines, with a growing presence in universities, bootcamps, and programming communities.” ISMOS was born in Latin America as Librería de Satoshi and is now a global movement.

One Million Bitcoin Developers Around the World

ISMOS combines rigorous study programs, direct mentorship, and fellowships in Spanish, Portuguese, and English, and soon in more languages. Subjects will include Bitcoin, cryptography, cybersecurity, mathematics, AI, Nostr, open-source software, and open AI models. The platform is open source, and software developers can explore its open tools at github.com/ismos-xyz.

Today ISMOS is primarily supported by Btrust and the Human Rights Foundation. Other organizations, such as OpenSats and the Gemini Opportunity Fund, have supported its work in the past with smaller grants, according to the press release.

The announcement reflects nearly five years of growth and a deeper commitment to equal opportunity. “Someone coding in Argentina, Nigeria, or El Salvador deserves the same chance to build a first-class technical career as anyone in Silicon Valley or London.”

ISMOS aims to go beyond study programs to provide individual support to the best developers through programs such as B4OS (Bitcoin 4 Open Source), fellowships, and its developer residencies: “in their language, at their level, and with the specific support they need to go further than they imagined.”

#5137. Anthropic's AI Is Getting Cheaper to Use. That's Becoming a Problem for Its Business

Anthropic's AI Is Getting Cheaper to Use. That's Becoming a Problem for Its Business

Anthropic is making Claude cheaper to use. Its computing bill, however, is moving in the other direction.

Anthropic said revenue growth from increased usage was "partially offset by a decrease of approximately $600 million from price reductions introduced as part of new model versions and contractual discounts," according to its amended SEC filing.

Meanwhile, compute and infrastructure expenses surged from $5.56 billion to $9.86 billion, an increase of roughly 77%.

That means Anthropic spent roughly 58 cents on compute and infrastructure for every dollar of revenue, versus 48 cents a quarter earlier. The measure includes computing used for research, training, and internal operations—not just serving paying Claude customers—so it isn't a per-prompt profit margin.

The $600 million figure isn't revenue that vanished from Anthropic's books. It's the amount the company says price reductions and discounts offset revenue growth driven by higher usage.

The cuts are not hypothetical. Claude Opus 5.5, which lowered token prices compared with Opus 5, was recently released, being more capable than any previous model, and sometimes even up to par against Fable. Anthropic also introduced Haiku 5.5 in October, pitching a much cheaper model for high-volume work.

Anthropic says Fable 5.1 reduced the cost of typical workloads by around 25%, while Opus 5.5 brought customers' cost per task down roughly 40% compared with Opus 5. The reductions reflect both lower prices and efficiency gains, rather than straight discounts across every task. Anthropic detailed Fable's lower cache-read pricing in its model announcement.

There is a business case for that strategy: cheaper, more capable AI can encourage customers to use more of it. Anthropic says users have historically expanded consumption after such releases.

But its latest quarter also shows how difficult it is to synchronize demand with supply. Anthropic typically reserves compute capacity 12 to 18 months before it becomes available, leaving much of that spending relatively fixed in the near term. It’s also infamous among AI enthusiasts because its quotas tend to deplete too easily.

The quarter included $5 billion of compute under short-term commitments that Anthropic says cost significantly more than comparable capacity secured through multiyear contracts. That expense helped push the company from a $974 million operating profit in the second quarter to a $567 million operating loss in the third.

The longer-term stakes are bigger. Anthropic's IPO filing, means the company is preparing to go public, and put the company in Wall Street’s bulls eye. Its updated disclosures put aggregate lease and purchasing commitments at roughly $895.4 billion, substantially all related to compute and infrastructure.

Reuters has also reported that the filing raised questions about whether infrastructure partners can secure the financing needed to deliver all that capacity. As of now, Google and Nvidia seem to be the most benefited from Anthropic’s growth as its core business depends on their infrastructure.

For now, demand for Claude is still growing rapidly. The harder question is whether Anthropic can keep making its models cheaper faster than the cost of building and running them comes down. Right now, OpenAI, which is also preparing its own IPO offers a competitive model, with many usage resets, and a more generous usage quota.

That’s the main issue keeping Anthropic from rising prices.

#5135. Jack Dorsey’s Block (XYZ) Sets Aside $764 Million for DOJ Settlement as Bitcoin Profit Halves

Jack Dorsey’s Block agreed in principle to a $764 million deferred-prosecution deal over anti-money-laundering failures at Cash App, a sum that exceeds its $566 million Q3 profit, while bitcoin gross profit fell 50% after the company cut trading fees.

Block has agreed in principle to pay $764 million to resolve a Justice Department investigation into its anti-money-laundering controls, a sum larger than the $566 million profit the company reported for the third quarter.

The agreement, reached in October and disclosed in a 10-Q filed Nov. 3, would defer for three years a criminal charge that Block failed to maintain an effective anti-money-laundering program under the Bank Secrecy Act.

The gross figure is about $964 million, reduced to $764 million after credits for earlier regulatory settlements. Block has accrued the full amount and said losses above it are “reasonably possible.”

The company disputes the basis and methodology of the government’s assessment, and the deal requires final approval.

The settlement overshadowed a quarter in which gross profit rose 22% to $3.24 billion, with Cash App up 27% to $2.07 billion and Square up 14% to $1.16 billion, according to the company release.

Bitcoin was the exception. Gross profit from the bitcoin business fell 50% to $52 million from $104 million a year earlier, and bitcoin revenue dropped 11% to $1.8 billion.

The investigation dates to March 2023, when Hindenburg Research alleged that Cash App inflated user counts with duplicate and fraudulent accounts and that weak identity checks let criminals use the platform for scams and money laundering. Block called the report inaccurate and misleading.

The Justice Department and SEC opened inquiries into the compliance practices and related disclosures; the SEC closed its side in March without recommending enforcement.

State regulators moved first. In April 2025 the New York Department of Financial Services fined Block $40 million after finding a backlog of suspicious-activity alerts that grew from about 18,000 in 2018 to more than 169,000 by 2020, and a screening system that did not block bitcoin transfers to wallets linked to terrorism financing until exposure passed 10%.

A multistate settlement in January 2025 added $80 million. Those payments account for part of the $200 million credit against the DOJ figure.

The deferred prosecution structure means Block avoids a conviction if it meets the agreement’s terms over three years, a path Binance took in 2023 at a cost of $4.3 billion.

The charge lands as Block pursues an industrial bank charter for a unit it calls Builders Bank, which would offer custody and fiduciary services for bitcoin. Bank regulators weigh compliance history in charter decisions.

The drop in bitcoin profit was a choice. Block said the decline came from its decision to cut fees on certain Cash App bitcoin transactions, part of a push to make the asset a payment rail rather than a trading product.

The company auto-enabled about 1 million Square merchants for Lightning payments in May, waived processing fees on bitcoin through 2026, and in October launched a national ad campaign built on spending bitcoin rather than holding it.

Revenue from bitcoin sales to customers, which Block books at gross, fell as the price dropped from about $114,000 to $70,000 over the year.

Block held 28,355 BTC across its treasury and customer balances as of the first quarter, including about 9,000 in the corporate treasury, and continues to put 10% of bitcoin gross profit into purchases.

Two $1,000 comparisons leave about 1 basis point and negative 15 before fees, while access and share adjustments complicate the trade.

Tokens tracking Nvidia shares can trade at different prices across issuers and exchanges, but buying the cheaper version and selling a dearer one leaves little room for profit in two modeled comparisons published by data provider Coin Metrics on Nov. 3.

The data provider's execution study shows about one basis point remaining in one $1,000 comparison after entry and exit slippage, and a negative 15 basis points in another.

The results show how a visible price difference can shrink when an order reaches the market, while preserving a small positive remainder in the first example.

A holder must compare the same share exposure, have something to sell on the expensive side, and qualify for the route used to settle the trade.

#5132. CFTC approves individual stock perpetual futures trading in US for the first time

Get The Block’s latest crypto news and price alerts for the coins you follow, right in Chrome. Add our free extension here.

Perpetual futures contracts surged in popularity over the past year, particularly after disruptions in global supply chains in the Middle East earlier this year at the onset of the war.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission approved the ability for exchanges in the United States to offer perpetual futures contracts tied to individual stocks — just months after those assets were put into the spotlight by President Donald Trump.

On Tuesday, CFTC Chair Michael Selig greenlit the ability to trade those perpetual futures contracts for the first time in the U.S. for platforms.

"This expansion marks a significant step towards allowing U.S. market participants, consistent with applicable law, to avail themselves of the advantages of perpetual futures that have led to their emergence as widely sought tools for risk-management and price-discovery," Selig said.

Perpetuals, or perps, are a type of futures contract that don't have an expiration date and allow people to bet on the price movement of assets without owning them directly.

Perpetual futures contracts surged in popularity over the past year, particularly after disruptions in global supply chains in the Middle East earlier this year at the onset of the war, after the U.S. and Israel conducted missile strikes on Iran, which triggered supply shocks. That happened over the weekend, so traditional oil futures markets were closed, but platforms like Hyperliquid operate 24/7, so much of the trading happened onchain.

Over the past year, the CFTC has approved a few perpetual futures contracts. The agency first opened the door for bitcoin perpetual futures contracts in the U.S. when its staff greenlit KalshiEX and Coinbase to list the products. Then in June, the CFTC released a request for comment on crude oil perpetual contracts and 24/7 trading.

Perpetuals futures contracts have also caught Trump's attention. In August, he said he wanted the CFTC to work to bring Hyperliquid into the U.S.

Both the SEC and CFTC would oversee the contracts, Selig said on Tuesday.

"This framework recognized the complementary roles of the CFTC and SEC in overseeing American financial markets by providing a pathway for innovation at the intersection of the U.S.," Selig said.

#5131. Strategy’s STRC Hits $100 Par for First Time Since May After Over $2 Billion in Buybacks

Strategy’s STRC preferred hit $100 par on Wednesday for the first time since May, after billions in buybacks, a 12% dividend rate and a switch to daily payouts.

Strategy’s Stretch preferred stock touched $100 today for the first time since May, returning to the par value the company has spent over $2 billion in buybacks and five months of rate increases to defend.

STRC traded below $80 at times in June, a massive discount to its stated value. The climb back to $100 restores the price at which Strategy says it will resume issuing new shares, the mechanism that funds its bitcoin purchases. Chairman Michael Saylor had pledged to keep the stock at or above par and to hold the dividend at 12% until it got there.

Two changes landed in the past week. Shareholders approved daily dividends on STRC and three other preferreds on Oct. 28 by a 99.3% vote, removing the semi-monthly ex-dividend drops that had added volatility to the price.

The first daily payment went out Monday. And Strategy’s Oct. 29 filing set the November rate at 12% annualized, or $1 per share for the month.

Shares of Strategy (MSTR) were up over 7% today after bitcoin jumped above $80,000.

BREAKING: Michael Saylor's STRC has returned to par for the first time since May! 👀They will start buying more bitcoin as soon as it goes above $100 🚀 pic.twitter.com/niNmngTP1j

Stretch, the Variable Rate Series A Perpetual Stretch Preferred, launched in July 2025 at $90 with a 9% starting rate. Saylor called it the company’s “iPhone moment.” The design is a feedback loop: Strategy adjusts the dividend each month to hold the price near $100, sells new shares when it trades above par and uses the cash to buy bitcoin.

It became the largest tradable preferred in the world, with a market value above $8 billion and a holder base that CEO Phong Le has put at about 80% retail.

The loop broke earlier this year. STRC drifted below par in late January; Strategy raised the rate to 11.25% in February, 11.5% in March and 12% by summer, and the price kept sliding as bitcoin fell toward $65,000. At $89 the at-the-market program sat idle, cutting off the company’s cheapest funding.

In late May, Strategy sold 32 BTC for about $2.5 million to cover a Stretch distribution, its first bitcoin sale since 2022, and critics raised the prospect of a “death spiral” that analysts at Benchmark and TD Cowen disputed.

The fix was to buy the stock back. Strategy paused bitcoin purchases in the week of Oct. 19 and spent $204.9 million on STRC alone, part of the roughly $2.25 billion it has retired since the discount opened.

Each share bought below $100 shrank the float and reduced the dividend bill at the same time.

The recovery matters because of what sits beneath it. Strategy holds 849,327 BTC after adding 811 coins last week, at an average cost of about $75,446. With bitcoin near $78,300 on Wednesday, the position is about 4% above water.

The company reported $20.91 billion in third-quarter operating income, almost all of it unrealized gains, alongside a negative year-to-date BTC yield and a chief financial officer stepping down.

The preferred stack is the bill that comes due regardless. STRC, STRF, STRK and STRD together carry annual dividends in the hundreds of millions, and the quarter’s 5,552 BTC in sales went to fund them and the buybacks. A Stretch at par lets Strategy pay those obligations with new preferred issuance rather than coins. A Stretch at $89 does not.

The test now is whether the company reopens the ATM at $100 and whether buyers absorb it.

#5130. Weekend stock tokens predict Monday open, but guessing up scores 55%

Bitquery’s pre-futures weekend test found no clear directional edge, while Nasdaq’s proposed weekday expansion remains conditional.

Stock tokens kept trading through weekends, but their prices did not reliably guide the next stock-market open in a new study of 121 stocks.

Blockchain data provider Bitquery's Nov. 3 analysis found that Sunday token moves measured before equity-index futures reopened correctly called 54% of qualifying openings, so simply predicting that every stock would open higher scored 55%.

More hours can give investors another opportunity to transact, but they do not show that the resulting prices predict the next opening better.

Bitquery followed 17 weekends beginning July 10 through Oct. 30, with the final stock opening on Nov. 2. It recorded 791 stock-opening observations across those stocks, and its direction test kept the 533 openings that moved at least 0.5% from Friday's close.

Token moves pointed the right way on 286 of those observations, compared with 291 correct calls for always predicting a rise. Because more openings rose than fell, a 50% coin-toss benchmark alone would flatter the tokens' result.

The study also used balanced accuracy, which averages success on rises and falls. The tokens scored 53%, with a reported 95% interval of 44% to 62%.

Thanks for signing up to The Catalyst. Look out for your first daily email. If you already receive it, you’re all set.

Across all 791 observations, including smaller moves, the median error was 1.2% using token moves versus 0.9% assuming the stock opened at Friday's close. Bitquery put the excess error at 0.3%, with a 95% range of 0.2% to 0.5%.

A weekend price is not yet a forecasting edge

Bitquery's study asks different questions about direction and forecast size. The later Sunday reading also changes the information and the sample.

Trading access and useful forecasting information remain separate claims.

Vendor research, not independent raw-data replication. No futures-price benchmark or cost-adjusted strategy. The later cutoff, volume floor and movement filter change together.

Method: Reported study figures only. Main test: 17 weekends beginning July 10–October 30, openings through November 2. Direction filters stock moves below 0.5%; size uses all 791 observations. Panel intervals are reported 95% ranges. Point and interval geometry maps linearly onto the same 40%–70% balanced-accuracy scale; this is an interval plot, not a zero-based bar chart.

The main test read token prices just before 6 p.m. Sunday ET, the futures reopening cutoff used by Bitquery. That timing is important because a later token price could incorporate information already available from equity-index futures.A separate check using prices just before 8 p.m. returned 59% balanced accuracy, with a 95% range of 53% to 65%, across 220 openings. But it also raised the weekend-volume threshold to $1 million and changed the movement filter.Listings needed at least $10,000 of weekend trading and a trade in the hour before each cutoff. For example, Kraken's xStocks disclosure excludes the US, Canada, UK and Australia, permits compatible-wallet withdrawals and says holders lack ownership and voting rights in the underlying shares.

The next useful evidence would hold timing and eligibility constant, compare against available market benchmarks, and measure executable results after costs. Until then, an available weekend price should not be mistaken for a demonstrated forecasting advantage.

#5128. Tether Holds 150,000 Bitcoin, CEO Says—About 50,000 More Than Its Reserve Report Shows

Tether Holds 150,000 Bitcoin, CEO Says—About 50,000 More Than Its Reserve Report Shows

Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino said the stablecoin giant now holds around 150,000 Bitcoin, worth roughly $11.5 billion at current prices, a figure that exceeds what the company’s own reserve disclosures imply by some 50,000 coins.

“We have give or take 150,000 bitcoin ourselves. It’s not much, but it’s honest work,” Ardoino said during a keynote at the Plan ₿ Forum in Lugano, Switzerland, the city where Tether has run a Bitcoin and stablecoin adoption program since 2022.

The claim is notable because it doesn’t square neatly with the paper trail. Tether’s third-quarter reserve attestation, which covers the assets backing its USDT stablecoin, lists $8.37 billion of Bitcoin valued at $83,621 per coin, implying roughly 100,060 BTC.

That leaves about 50,000 coins, worth close to $3.8 billion, that its public filings do not yet account for. Ardoino did not say where the additional Bitcoin is held or when it was acquired, so his comment doesn’t indicate a fresh purchase of that size, and Tether has long maintained that its corporate Bitcoin investments sit separately from the reserves supporting USDT.

The stablecoin issuer has been accumulating Bitcoin for years. In May 2023, Tether said it would funnel up to 15% of its net realized operating profits into Bitcoin, and that it would custody the coins itself rather than rely on third-party custodians.

The strategy has been fueled by staggering profits: the company reported $1.5 billion in net operating profit in the third quarter alone, and it has posted billion-dollar quarterly profits throughout the year while its USDT supply has kept growing.

The broader reserve picture, as laid out in the Q3 report, shows $191.45 billion in assets against $183.50 billion in liabilities, leaving an excess cushion of $7.95 billion, nearly double the $4.11 billion buffer it reported in June. U.S. Treasury bills remain the bulk of reserves at about $132.4 billion.

The transparency gap is a sensitive subject for Tether, which has faced years of scrutiny over whether USDT is fully backed. The company began its first full financial audit with KPMG this year, a long-awaited step toward addressing those doubts.

Ardoino also used the Lugano stage to tout Tether’s scale, saying the company now serves more than 730 million users worldwide and is adding roughly 30 million wallets a quarter, as he pitched a suite of open-source technologies funded by its profits.

#5127. Justin Sun seeks sanctions against World Liberty, alleging Trump-linked firm hid UAE ties

Get The Block’s latest crypto news and price alerts for the coins you follow, right in Chrome. Add our free extension here.

The dispute over World Liberty's citizenship emerged after the company amended an initial court disclosure that had listed only one entity in its ownership chain and Florida as its sole citizenship.

Tron founder Justin Sun said Tuesday he has filed a motion seeking sanctions against World Liberty Financial, alleging the DeFi protocol failed to disclose its United Arab Emirates citizenship until months into their legal dispute.

Sun, who says he invested $45 million in WLFI tokens, sued the Trump-linked crypto venture in April, accusing it of fraud and unlawfully freezing his tokens.

The dispute over World Liberty's citizenship emerged after the company amended an initial court disclosure that had listed only one entity in its ownership chain and Florida as its sole citizenship. In a subsequent filing, World Liberty identified 22 members in its ownership chain and claimed citizenship in Florida, Delaware, Puerto Rico, and the UAE, according to Sun.

Sun alleges the late disclosure was an attempt to challenge the federal court's jurisdiction and push the case out of open court. World Liberty was "proudly" American when selling tokens, he said, but discovered its UAE roots "only when it needed a way out of an American federal courtroom."

Under federal diversity jurisdiction rules, Sun argued, his case could proceed in federal court only if he and World Liberty were citizens of different jurisdictions. Because a company takes on the citizenship of its owners for these purposes, World Liberty's UAE ties could undermine the court's jurisdiction.

Sun said he plans to refile the lawsuit in California state court after the sanctions motion is resolved.

In May, World Liberty Financial countersued Sun, accusing him of running a "meritless PR stunt" against the Trump-family-backed crypto project after his tokens were frozen.

World Liberty debuted in October 2024 amid significant scrutiny because of its association with President Donald Trump and his family. The WLFI token reached an all-time high of around $0.33 and currently trades near $0.051, giving it a fully diluted valuation of approximately $5.1 billion.

#5125. Matt Corallo Flags Critical Linux Kernel Flaw; Lightning Labs Ships LND Mitigation

Bitcoin Core and Lightning developer Matt Corallo highlighted a severe Linux kernel vulnerability on October 30, criticizing Ubuntu’s delayed response to what he called “the most critical Linux vuln ever.” The bug, tracked as CVE-2026-98432, affects the kernel’s IPv4 TCP handshake code with a CVSS severity score of 9.8. Anthropic’s Frontier Red Team later showed it could be turned into a remote root exploit against systems exposing a Multipath TCP (MPTCP) listener.

Peter Todd echoed the warning the same day, advising anyone running LND on Linux with open ports to shut their Bitcoin Lightning nodes down until the kernel was patched or otherwise mitigated. The demonstrated exploit path relies on an MPTCP listener—something Go 1.24 and later enable by default. Because LND is written in Go, recent versions were listening with MPTCP on their peer, gRPC, and REST ports whenever the kernel had the feature enabled.

Lightning Labs responded the same day with emergency releases: lnd v0.21.6-beta and the backport v0.20.7-beta. Both disable MPTCP listeners by default, closing the demonstrated exploit path through LND. The project described the change as a mitigation, not a fix, and noted that only a patched kernel fully resolves the underlying issue. Other services on the same machine remain exposed until MPTCP is disabled host-wide or the kernel is updated. Olaoluwa Osuntokun and the official Lightning Labs account both recommended the update.

Security researcher Marcus Hutchins later reported internet-wide scanning activity consistent with threat actors looking for exposed systems. His scans found roughly 2.1 million servers reachable over MPTCP on port 443. International Cyber Digest amplified the finding on November 4, noting the scanning and Ubuntu’s slower patch timeline.

Canonical has since made fixed kernels available in the opt-in, proposed pocket for Ubuntu 22.04, 24.04, and 26.04, but they have not yet reached the regular updates channel. Red Hat shipped fixes for RHEL 8/9/10 on November 1; Debian, Amazon Linux, and others had already released patches earlier.

UmbrelOS 2.0.1 included the kernel fix on November 1st for x86 devices and applied a traffic-blocking mitigation on Raspberry Pi, where a fixed kernel was not yet available. No confirmed in-the-wild exploitation has been reported, and the vulnerability has not been added to CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. Anthropic’s remote-root demonstration remains unpublished.

The practical exposure is highest on internet-facing servers. Home desktop systems behind typical NAT and firewalls, without public TCP listeners, are far less affected. For Lightning operators on Linux, the LND releases remove the specific MPTCP listener path the public exploit used, but the broader kernel bug remains until a patched kernel is installed.

On Tuesday, Polymarket users gave Democrats a 76% chance of securing the Senate, and the House a 94% chance.

Ahead of polls closing in the U.S. midterm elections, bettors on prediction market platforms are increasingly pricing in Democrats taking both the House and Senate.

As of early Tuesday afternoon, Polymarket users gave Democrats a 76% chance of securing the Senate, and the House a 94% chance. Similarly, on Kalshi, bettors said Democrats had a 94% chance of controlling the House and a 75% chance for the Senate. All 435 House seats are up for election, as well as 35 of the 100 Senate seats.

Prediction markets surged in popularity during the 2024 presidential election, emerging as an alternative barometer of public opinion and drawing comparisons to national polling. Since then, platforms like Polymarket and Kalshi have generated significant revenue and reached multibillion-dollar valuations.

But interest in election-related trading has cooled considerably since 2024, according to a Bloomberg report published Tuesday. Politics accounted for just 1% of trading volume on both Kalshi and Polymarket in October, down from more than 60% during the 2024 election, Bloomberg reported.

A shift in parties is pivotal since Democrats are likely to then lead key committees, driving the agenda. For crypto, that could mean that Democrats such as Elizabeth Warren and Sherrod Brown could lead panels overseeing the digital asset industry.

Experts who spoke with The Block last month said that would mean more oversight over key issues, including President Donald Trump's crypto wealth through his family's World Liberty Financial, and less of an emphasis on crypto legislation.

As for key crypto races, such as Ohio, where incumbent Jon Husted will face off against crypto critic and former Sen. Brown, bettors on Kalshi say Brown has a 71% chance of beating Husted. For other races, including lawmakers focused on crypto legislation, Sen. Cory Booker, D.-N.J. has a 98% chance on Kalshi.

#5122. French bank resumes transfers after $133 million attack but leaves crypto loss unconfirmed

Arkéa says attackers used its own account through a provider's platform, while a separate $108.8 million USDC trail leaves the bank-to-crypto link unproven.

French bank Crédit Mutuel Arkéa said almost all operations had resumed on Nov. 4 after an attack enabled fraudulent crypto transactions from its own account, delaying some customer transfers.

In a later clarification, the bank said attackers reached it through a service provider's platform and sent money to other banks. Those transactions may then have enabled conversion into cryptocurrency through specialized platforms.

Arkéa did not confirm that conversion or connect its transfers to specific crypto wallets.

The bank denied that the attack entered through Fortuneo, its online banking subsidiary, and said it did not use customer accounts. It described the incident as contained and said customers' holdings were unaffected.

Arkéa declined to confirm whether €118 million ($133 million) had been stolen and validated only their order of magnitude. It said some funds had been blocked and further recovery efforts were underway, making a definitive financial amount premature.

The amount involved in fraudulent transactions is not necessarily the bank's final loss once blocked funds and recoveries are accounted for. Arkéa said the sums would not threaten its financial strength.

Its initial statement described precautionary transaction suspensions and a gradual restart after checks and stronger security measures. The later update said almost all operations had resumed during the morning.

Arkéa said it was working with judicial and police authorities to determine the attack's origin and method.

Separately, blockchain analytics firm Bitquery reported tracing $108.8 million in USDC withdrawals from wallets it labels as belonging to Kraken, Crypto.com and OKX to 15 addresses on Nov. 1 and 2. The withdrawals ran from 12:25 UTC on Nov. 1 to 09:09 UTC the next day, roughly 21 hours.

#5120. CZ calls for crypto security alliance as AI-driven attacks accelerate after Binance hack

Get The Block’s latest crypto news and price alerts for the coins you follow, right in Chrome. Add our free extension here.

Changpeng Zhao says companies need AI-based defenses and an industry alliance to share lessons and freeze stolen funds faster, in his first interview since the Oct. 29 hack.

Binance cofounder and former CEO Changpeng "CZ" Zhao said AI is accelerating cyberattacks and argued companies should invest in AI-based defenses, security personnel, and partnerships with AI security providers.

In his first public interview since the Oct. 29 hack of Binance, Zhao told the Talking Tokens podcast that the threat extends beyond individual companies to the broader crypto industry and global financial system, given crypto's connections to stablecoins, tokenized stocks, real-world assets, and traditional finance.

"The speed of hacking is going to pick up because of AI capabilities [being] so strong now. At the same time, we've got to use more AI to defend. The only way to fight a monster is to kind of become that monster."

The comments come amid a string of security incidents across the crypto industry, including a separate AI-assisted breach at blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis and a $46 million security incident at Brazilian exchange Mercado Bitcoin.

Zhao said he learned of the incident around midnight in the UAE and focused on communicating with the community while Binance's team worked to contain the attack and protect users. He attributed relatively calm market conditions and subsequent net inflows to the company's response, financial capacity and user trust. He described security incidents as preventable with sufficient effort and attention, while warning that organizations can become complacent.

Earlier Tuesday, Binance said hackers used a fake job interview to compromise an employee's computer before leveraging an internal AI tool in the attack. The exchange also said it detected and prevented 57 suspected North Korea-linked cyber threats in 2026.

Zhao called for an industry alliance to share lessons and best practices, conduct cross-audits and help freeze stolen funds more quickly. He views security as an ongoing process rather than a milestone that must be reached before adoption.

"As an industry, I encourage [...] forming some kind of industry alliance on security to help each other learn from each other's mistakes, share the best practices, cross audits, help each other freeze funds very quickly, etc."

Zhao said he had not spoken with President Donald Trump or other U.S. officials about the incident, but that Binance and the broader crypto industry would welcome government assistance. Trump has said the U.S. was "looking into it."

"What's bad for crypto on this scale has real economic impact elsewhere," Zhao said. "So you cannot just say, 'Look, this is one specific problem for one specific sector or for one specific company.' It impacts the company, impacts the industry, impacts global finance. It's all interconnected, and I think, given the size of impact, it's definitely at the national security level as well."

Zhao expressed optimism that AI could help identify software vulnerabilities and strengthen defenses, while blockchain could support faster transactions facilitated by AI.
